hook: Doctors track how fast a medicine's concentration falls, economists how fast cost grows with each extra unit, ecologists how fast a population spreads. The derivative is the same in all of them; what changes is the story and the units. This topic practices reading rates, and rates of rates, in many settings.

chain.cause: Any quantity $Q$ that depends on an input
chain.effect: has a rate of change $Q'$ in units of $Q$ per unit of input
says whether the quantity is increasing or decreasing

chain.cause: $Q'$ is itself a function, so $Q''$ is the rate of change of the rate
chain.effect: measured in units of Q per input unit per input unit
says whether the rate $Q'$ is increasing or decreasing

ideas: An interpretation names the input value, the quantity, increasing or decreasing, and the rate with units.
When the function is itself a rate (liters per hour), its derivative is a rate of a rate (liters per hour per hour).
$Q' < 0$ with $Q'' > 0$: decreasing, but more slowly. $Q' > 0$ with $Q'' < 0$: increasing, but more slowly.
Chained quantities multiply rates, and their units cancel: (°F per foot)(feet per minute) = °F per minute.

misconception.wrong: If $H''(t) > 0$, the temperature is going up.
misconception.right: $H''$ describes the rate $H'$, not the temperature. With $H' < 0$ and $H'' > 0$ the temperature is still falling, just more slowly.

summary: In any context, $Q'$ is the rate of change of $Q$ in units of $Q$ per input unit, and $Q''$ is the rate of change of that rate. Read the sign of $Q'$ for increasing or decreasing and the sign of $Q''$ for whether that rate grows or shrinks. Always state units.
